content: Cholesterol is a sterol, which is a combination of a steroid and an alcohol. It is a lipid that is present in the cell membranes of all tissues and is transported in the blood plasma of all animals. Cholesterol is synthesized by all eukaryotes, and trace amounts can also be found in the membranes of plants and fungi. The term cholesterol originates from the Greek words chole(bile) and stereos (solid), with the suffix -ol denoting an alcohol. It was first identified in solid form in gallstones by François Poulletier de la Salle in 1769. However, it was not until 1815 that the compound was named cholesterine by chemist Eugène Chevreul. Most cholesterol is synthesized by the body, although some is derived from dietary sources. Cholesterol is more abundant in tissues that either synthesize it in greater quantities or have densely packed membranes, such as the liver, spinal cord, and brain. It plays a critical role in various biochemical processes, including the composition of cell membranes and the synthesis of steroid hormones. Cholesterol is insoluble in blood and is transported in the circulatory system bound to lipoproteins, which are spherical particles with an exterior primarily composed of water-soluble proteins. The main types of lipoproteins are low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and high-density lipoprotein (HDL), which transport cholesterol to and from the liver. Elevated cholesterol levels (hypercholesterolemia) and abnormal proportions of LDL and HDL are associated with cardiovascular disease, as they promote the development of atheromas in arteries (atherosclerosis). This process can lead to myocardial infarction (heart attack), stroke, and peripheral vascular disease. LDL is often referred to as bad cholesterol because of its role in this process, while HDL is considered good cholesterol due to its protective effects. The balance of LDL and HDL can be improved through exercise, a healthy diet, and sometimes medication. Cholesterol is essential for building and maintaining cell membranes, as it regulates membrane fluidity across a wide range of temperatures. Its hydroxyl group interacts with the phosphate head of the membrane, while the bulky steroid and hydrocarbon chain are embedded within the membrane. Some research suggests that cholesterol may act as an antioxidant. It also aids in the production of bile, which is stored in the gallbladder and helps digest fats, and is important for the metabolism of fat-soluble vitamins, including vitamins A, D, E, and K. Cholesterol is the primary precursor for the synthesis of vitamin D and various steroid hormones, such as cortisol, aldosterone, and sex hormones like progesterone, estrogens, and testosterone. Recent studies have implicated cholesterol in cell signaling processes, where it may form lipid rafts in the plasma membrane. It also reduces the permeability of the plasma membrane to hydrogen ions (protons) and sodium ions. Cholesterol is crucial for the structure and function of invaginated caveolae and clathrin-coated pits, which are involved in caveolae-dependent and clathrin-dependent endocytosis. The role of cholesterol in these processes can be studied by using methyl-beta-cyclodextrin (MβCD) to remove cholesterol from the plasma membrane. Cholesterol is synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum of mammalian cells or obtained from the diet, where it is delivered by the bloodstream in low-density lipoproteins (LDL). These LDL particles are taken into cells via LDL receptor-mediated endocytosis in clathrin-coated pits and then hydrolyzed in lysosomes. Cholesterol is primarily synthesized from acetyl-CoA through the HMG-CoA reductase pathway in many cells and tissues. Approximately 20–25% of total daily cholesterol production (~1 g/day) occurs in the liver, with other sites of high synthesis rates including the intestines, adrenal glands, and reproductive organs. For an average person weighing about 150 pounds (68 kg), the total body cholesterol content is approximately 35 g, with a typical daily internal production of about 1 g and a dietary intake of 200–300 mg in the United States and similar dietary patterns. Of the cholesterol input to the intestines via bile production, 92–97% is reabsorbed and recycled through enterohepatic circulation. Konrad Bloch and Feodor Lynen were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1964 for their discoveries regarding the mechanism and regulation of cholesterol and fatty acid metabolism. The biosynthesis of cholesterol is directly regulated by cholesterol levels through homeostatic mechanisms, although these are not fully understood. Higher dietary intake leads to a net decrease in endogenous production, while lower intake has the opposite effect. The main regulatory mechanism involves the sensing of intracellular cholesterol in the endoplasmic reticulum by the protein SREBP (Sterol Regulatory Element Binding Protein 1 and 2). In the presence of cholesterol, SREBP is bound to two other proteins: SCAP (SREBP-cleavage activating protein) and Insig-1. When cholesterol levels fall, Insig-1 dissociates from the SREBP-SCAP complex, allowing the complex to migrate to the Golgi apparatus, where SREBP is cleaved by S1P and S2P (site 1/2 protease), two enzymes activated by SCAP when cholesterol levels are low. The cleaved SREBP then migrates to the nucleus and acts as a transcription factor to bind to the SRE (sterol regulatory element) of various genes to stimulate their transcription. Among the genes transcribed are the LDL receptor and HMG-CoA reductase. The former scavenges circulating LDL from the bloodstream, while HMG-CoA reductase increases endogenous cholesterol production. Much of this mechanism was elucidated by Dr. Michael S. Brown and Dr. Joseph L. Goldstein in the 1970s, who received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work in 1985. Cholesterol is excreted from the liver in bile and reabsorbed from the intestines. Under certain conditions, when more concentrated, such as in the gallbladder, it crystallizes and is the major constituent of most gallstones, although lecithin and bilirubin gallstones also occur less frequently. Cholesterol is minimally soluble in water and cannot dissolve or travel in the water-based bloodstream. Instead, it is transported in the bloodstream by lipoproteins, which are protein molecular suitcases that are water-soluble and carry cholesterol and triglycerides internally. The apolipoproteins forming the surface of a given lipoprotein particle determine from which cells cholesterol will be removed and to where it will be supplied. The largest lipoproteins, which primarily transport fats from the intestinal mucosa to the liver, are called chylomicrons. They carry mostly fats in the form of triglycerides and cholesterol. In the liver, chylomicron particles release triglycerides and some cholesterol. The liver converts unburned food metabolites into very low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) and secretes them into plasma, where they are converted to low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles and non-esterified fatty acids, which can affect other body cells. In healthy individuals, the relatively few LDL particles are large. In contrast, large numbers of small dense LDL (sdLDL) particles are strongly associated with the presence of atheromatous disease within the arteries. For this reason, LDL is referred to as bad cholesterol.
